To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the detection thresholds of the linear and angular components of curved-path motion were not independent, and that the detection thresholds for the linear component increased with the magnitude of the concurrent angular velocity.

(1) during curved-path motion, the detection threshold for linear motion increases with increasing magnitude of simultaneous angular velocity; (2) during curved-path rotation, the detection threshold of angular velocity is only slightly increased with increasing linear velocity; and (3) the interaction between the two sensory systems is not symmetric, with a stronger interaction between the linear velocity and angular velocity components of curved-path motion than between the angular velocity and linear velocity components of curved path motion.
the perception of linear and angular velocity during curved-path motion is based on the interaction of canal and otolith signals.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the vestibular system is not a collection of independent detectors for angular and linear motion.
the vestibular system is not able to process linear and rotational components of self-motion independently.
during curved path motion, the otoliths and semicircular canalis interact extensively for accurate tilt and inertial estimates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human perceptual system is not a simple linear filter of sensory information, and that the way we perceive the world around us may be more complicated than we think.
the vestibular system may not provide a clean signal of linear acceleration to the brain.
the human vestibular system does not have independent access, through conscious perception, to estimates of linear and rotational motion parameters during curved-path self motion.
